title: Construction workers: building the nation without a roof of their own
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Construction workers and the welfare cess: the 1996 laws, the unspent crores, the Labour Codes, and what BMS and its construction federation ask for.
body:
Construction is among the largest employers in the unorganised sector, and also one of the most dangerous. The people who lay bricks, mix concrete, bend steel, carry loads up scaffolding and fit electrical lines for others to live and work in often have no permanent employer, no fixed place of work and no certificate to prove they are workers at all. BMS has a dedicated federation for them, the **Akhil Bharatiya Construction Mazdoor Mahasangh**. This post explains the legal framework meant to protect construction workers, the large sums collected for their welfare, the problems that persist and BMS's position.

## The legal framework

Two laws were passed in 1996. The **Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act** dealt with safety, health and working conditions on sites. The companion **Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Cess Act** created a source of money. It allows the levy of a cess on the cost of construction, which, according to the figures reported, has been fixed at one per cent. The proceeds are paid into State welfare boards, which register workers and spend the money on benefits such as education grants for children, medical help, maternity benefit, pension and accident cover.

The idea is a fair one: the value of every building includes the labour of the people who built it, so a small share of that value is set aside for the workers' welfare, and the worker does not depend on the goodwill of a contractor who may be gone next month.

The thresholds are worth knowing. As a Drishti IAS summary of the law records, the Act applies to establishments with ten or more construction workers, private residential projects below Rs 10 lakh were excluded, and sites with more than 500 workers must have emergency action plans.

## The law is changing

The two 1996 Acts are now part of the new Labour Codes, which came into force on 21 November 2025. The Cess Act is subsumed in the **Code on Social Security**, and the regulation Act is among the 13 laws merged into the **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code**. Under the Social Security Code, the cess is now levied under Section 100. A gazette notification dated 8 May 2026 specifies a cess of one per cent of the cost of construction and supersedes the earlier notification of 26 September 1996.

Commentators have raised a concern about one feature of the new scheme, the possibility that cess collection will rely more on employers' own assessment of construction cost, which they say could weaken collections. The Social Security Code also allows for portability of benefits through an Aadhaar-linked account number, a feature that matters for migrant workers, though the Ministry has described it chiefly in the context of gig and platform workers.

## The numbers

The scale of the cess is large, and so are the unspent balances. According to a Business Standard report of April 2023, which relied on a Parliament reply, up to November 2022 the boards had collected Rs 87,478 crore, spent Rs 49,269 crore, or 56 per cent, and left Rs 38,209 crore, or 44 per cent, unutilised. About 5.06 crore workers were registered with the boards. The same report showed wide differences between States: Kerala spent more than it collected, at 160.5 per cent, while Assam spent 18.7 per cent, Delhi 28.2 per cent and **West Bengal 35.7 per cent**.

A later summary by Drishti IAS, from January 2025, cites an RTI reply showing Rs 70,744 crore unspent across State boards, and notes that a labour economist's estimate for the period before the pandemic was that States distributed only 15 to 20 per cent of collections. The two sets of figures were compiled differently and for different dates, so they should not be added or compared directly, but they point in the same direction.

## Problems that persist

- **Unspent cess.** Large balances in several States, as the above figures show, while workers wait for benefits.
- **Slow registration and renewal.** The Business Standard report notes that boards rarely take the initiative to enrol workers, and that earlier rules required a certificate from an MP or a contractor, which left many workers outside. Self-enrolment is now permitted after 90 days of construction work in a year.
- **Diversion of funds.** The report quotes a construction workers' federation official as saying that funds are often diverted to other schemes and projects.
- **Poor safety.** The Drishti summary notes weak enforcement of provisions for accommodation, water and sanitation.
- **Administrative gaps.** A Comptroller and Auditor General audit of the Delhi board for 2019-20 to 2022-23, reported in The Tribune, found that the board claimed 6.96 lakh registered workers but could provide complete data for only 1.98 lakh, that cess figures reported by district authorities and the board differed by Rs 204.95 crore, that only 12 of 17 approved schemes were implemented, and that applications faced delays of up to 1,423 days.

Behind these figures is an ordinary experience: a worker injured on a site, a woman waiting for maternity benefit, a family waiting for a child's scholarship, finding that the card that was meant to be proof of entitlement leads to a closed counter.

## What BMS says

BMS has asked that welfare board funds be used only for workers, that registration be simple, and that site safety be enforced. The federation has also asked for a **national register** that follows the worker when she moves between States, a demand that makes particular sense for a workforce that is constantly on the move. It also supports the use of the cess to deliver benefits promptly, and argues that States which hold large balances should explain why the money has not reached those it was collected for.

## What remains to be done

- **Spend the money for the purpose.** Boards should disburse accumulated balances through schemes that workers can actually use.
- **Simplify registration.** Self-enrolment, digital cards and camps at work sites reduce dependence on middlemen.
- **Make benefits portable.** A worker who moves from West Bengal to Maharashtra for a job should not lose entitlements.
- **Enforce safety rules** at sites, especially large ones.
- **Audit and publish.** Regular audits, as in the Delhi case, and publication of board accounts allow workers' representatives to see what is happening.

For construction workers, a card is not a favour. It is the key to the benefits that their own work has paid for.
